title: QR-Map: A Map-Based Approach to Quantum Circuit Abstraction for Qubit Reuse Optimization
problem: Identifying optimal qubit reuse opportunities in quantum circuits via mid-circuit measurements is NP-hard in the general case; existing frameworks either suffer from exponential search complexity or produce non-optimal results due to non-deterministic heuristics.
method: QR-Map abstracts computational dependencies by extracting and aligning two-qubit gates into a map structure, making dependency detection deterministic and tractable. The framework identifies qubit reuse opportunities by analyzing these aligned gate maps, ensuring qubit savings without introducing excessive idle time. It jointly optimizes gate serialization depth and crosstalk reduction, balancing circuit fidelity with hardware constraints through a deterministic, polynomial-time map-based search.

title: Reuse-Aware Compilation for Zoned Quantum Architectures Based on Neutral Atoms
problem: Neutral-atom quantum computers use heterogeneous zoned architectures (storage, entangling, readout zones), and compiling quantum circuits for them requires efficiently managing qubit movement between zones to minimize fidelity-degrading data movement overhead.
method: ZAC (Zoned Architecture Compiler) introduces qubit reuse as a core optimization: qubits already in the entanglement zone are kept there if an immediate entangling gate is pending, avoiding round-trip movement to storage. ZAC additionally introduces novel data placement strategies that anticipate future gate scheduling needs, a new instruction scheduling algorithm for zoned operations, a flexible specification language for diverse zoned architectures, and ZAIR, an intermediate representation capturing zoned-architecture-specific constraints. The compiler is evaluated on circuits showing 22x fidelity improvement over monolithic architectures.

title: M-ANT: Efficient Low-bit Group Quantization for LLMs via Mathematically Adaptive Numerical Type
problem: Existing adaptive data types for LLM group quantization provide adaptivity at the tensor level, but small quantization groups within the same tensor exhibit markedly different distributions that tensor-level formats cannot accommodate. Additionally, dynamically generated KV caches require efficient real-time quantization that existing approaches do not support well.
method: MANT defines a mathematically adaptive numeric type with a flexible encoding paradigm covering a wider range of data distributions than prior adaptive types. A hardware framework assigns the appropriate MANT variant to each quantization group dynamically. A dedicated processing element (PE) fuses decoding and computation, and a real-time quantization unit handles dynamic KV cache quantization. These PEs are integrated into a systolic array, unifying weight and KV cache quantization in a single datapath.

title: MDPeek: Breaking Balanced Branches in SGX with Memory Disambiguation Unit Side Channels
problem: Intel SGX enclaves are believed to be protected against control-flow side-channel attacks when software defenses balance branch execution paths; this paper discovers that the Memory Disambiguation Unit (MDU) inside modern Intel CPUs leaks information even through these balanced branches, creating a previously unknown side channel.
method: MDPeek exploits the Memory Disambiguation Unit, a microarchitectural structure that speculatively allows or stalls dependent loads/stores based on address aliasing predictions. By crafting enclave access patterns that cause the MDU to make different predictions for secret-dependent branches (even when those branches are balanced at the instruction level), the attacker can observe MDU state changes through timing differences in a co-located spy process. The attack methodology reverse-engineers MDU behavior in Intel CPUs and demonstrates end-to-end information leakage from SGX enclaves.

title: PAISE: PIM-Accelerated Inference Scheduling Engine for Transformer-based LLM
problem: LLM inference on GPUs is memory-bound due to the attention layer's low arithmetic intensity and high memory traffic from frequent KV-cache updates, leading to elevated latency under autoregressive token generation. GPU-only execution under-utilizes available bandwidth for attention operations.
method: PAISE offloads memory-intensive attention operations from an AMD MI100 GPU to HBM-PIM devices via a GPU-PIM heterogeneous scheduling framework. A scheduling algorithm determines per-operation offload decisions based on model configuration (layer type, head count) and PIM hardware specifications (bandwidth, FLOPS). An enhanced PIM kernel implements transaction-wise interleave-batched GEMM, restructuring data layout so multiple attention heads' KV reads are interleaved across PIM banks, maximizing memory-level parallelism within the HBM-PIM device.

title: NeuVSA: A Unified and Efficient Accelerator for Neural Vector Search
problem: Neural Vector Search (NVS) systems require both a neural embedding stage and a vector search stage, but existing accelerators treat these as separate compute kernels with incompatible memory access patterns, causing insufficient parallelization, frequent data access conflicts, and poor scheduling.
method: NeuVSA uses Product Quantization (PQ) as a unifying computational primitive, reformulating both the embedding and search stages into the same computing and memory access paradigm via a learned PQ-based algorithm with end-to-end joint training of the codebook and index. The hardware is a homogeneous ASIC with multiple sub-accelerators, each exploiting all exposed parallelism through a structured index assignment strategy and an elastic on-chip buffer that prevents data access conflicts. A hardware-aware scheduling strategy coordinates sub-accelerators to maximize throughput. The joint training strategy improves recall by 4.6% and accuracy by 43.5% over LUT-NN.

title: Constant-Rate Entanglement Distillation for Fast Quantum Interconnects
problem: Existing quantum interconnect protocols cannot simultaneously achieve high fidelity and high rate of entanglement generation under realistic noisy local operations, creating a fundamental bottleneck for distributed quantum computing and blind quantum computation. Current entanglement distillation methods either have vanishing rate or fail to tolerate the noise levels present in physical systems.
method: The work develops a constant-rate entanglement distillation protocol using a sequence of two-way entanglement distillation rounds based on quantum error-detecting codes with increasing code rate. The scheme combines these iterated two-way distillation protocols with standard fault-tolerance techniques to achieve a net constant fraction of the raw entanglement pairs being converted to high-fidelity logical pairs. Numerical optimization is applied to minimize practical overhead given finite memory constraints.

title: Gaussian Blending Unit: An Edge GPU Plug-in for Real-Time Gaussian-Based Rendering in AR/VR
problem: 3D Gaussian Splatting on edge GPUs (e.g., Jetson Orin NX) achieves only 7-17 FPS for AR/VR rendering, far below the 60+ FPS threshold for immersive experiences, because the Gaussian Blending Stage—computing each Gaussian's contribution at every pixel—dominates compute time and is poorly suited to conventional GPU pipelines.
method: GBU is an edge GPU plug-in hardware module for the Gaussian Blending Stage. It introduces an intra-row sequential shading (IRSS) dataflow that processes pixels left-to-right within each row, using a two-step coordinate transformation that: (1) shares intermediate coordinate values between adjacent pixels, reducing per-pixel computation by up to 5.5x, and (2) enables early termination of Gaussians contributing minimally to pixels, reducing per-pixel computation by up to 93%. GBU adds a dedicated rendering engine that aggregates computations from multiple Gaussians across rows to balance workload. A Gaussian Reuse Cache reduces off-chip memory accesses by 44.9%. GBU integrates with conventional edge GPUs to support a wide range of AR/VR applications.

title: LLM.265: Video Codecs are Secretly Tensor Codecs
problem: LLM training and inference are increasingly bottlenecked by memory footprint and communication bandwidth for weights, activations, gradients, and KV cache, but existing tensor-compression methods are specialized for only one type of tensor and require custom hardware or software stacks. A unified, bandwidth-efficient compression mechanism applicable across all LLM tensor types is missing.
method: LLM.265 repurposes existing GPU hardware video encoders/decoders (H.265/HEVC engines) as general-purpose tensor codecs. The key insight is that LLM tensors expose spatial and temporal statistical structure (smooth weight manifolds, slowly changing activations, correlated KV cache vectors) that codec stages — inter-frame prediction, DCT/transform coding, scalar quantization, and entropy coding via context-adaptive arithmetic coding — can exploit directly. The system maps tensor layouts to frame formats, applies intra/inter prediction to exploit tensor correlations, and uses entropy coding to compress residuals. Custom hardware extensions to the existing video engine improve tensor encoding/decoding throughput without major GPU architecture changes.

title: AutoRFM: Scaling Low-Cost in-DRAM Trackers to Ultra-Low Rowhammer Thresholds
problem: In-DRAM Rowhammer mitigation using the DDR5 Refresh Management (RFM) command stalls the entire DRAM bank for 200-400ns per invocation; at ultra-low Rowhammer thresholds (sub-100), the required RFM frequency causes up to 33% performance slowdown with existing low-cost trackers such as MINT.
method: AutoRFM performs transparent RFM at the subarray granularity rather than the full bank level: it targets only one subarray at a time for mitigation while all other subarrays continue to service requests uninterrupted. If an activation request arrives for the subarray currently under mitigation, the DRAM chip issues an ALERT signal to the Memory Controller to retry after a bounded 200ns wait. Randomized Memory Mapping breaks spatial correlation between consecutive bank accesses to prevent repeated targeting of the same subarray. A Fractal Mitigation Algorithm handles transitive Rowhammer attacks (e.g., Half-Double) without recursive same-subarray mitigations. The design is evaluated with SPEC, GAP, and stream workloads.

title: ShadowLoad: Injecting State into Hardware Prefetchers
problem: Hardware prefetchers in modern CPUs maintain internal state (e.g., stride tables, stream detectors) that persists across security boundaries, and prior work showed this state leaks information across processes, user/kernel space, and trusted execution environments (TEEs). This paper extends the threat by demonstrating that an attacker can actively inject crafted state into a victim's prefetcher, turning it into a covert communication channel or an amplification primitive.
method: ShadowLoad crafts memory access sequences that train the hardware prefetcher's internal prediction structures (stride tables, stream buffers) to a desired state from an unprivileged attacker context. When the victim process subsequently executes, the pre-injected prefetcher state causes speculative prefetches that alter the victim's cache state or execution timing, enabling state injection across process, user-kernel, and TEE boundaries. The technique exploits the fact that prefetcher state is not flushed or partitioned at privilege transitions on affected CPUs.

title: Embracing Imbalance: Dynamic Load Shifting among Microservice Containers in Shared Clusters
problem: Containers within the same microservice deployed in large shared clusters experience temporal and spatial performance imbalance due to resource contention; standard load-balancing policies assume homogeneous container performance and respond with over-provisioning, wasting resources while still frequently violating SLAs.
method: The paper proposes dynamic load shifting, a system that continuously monitors per-container performance metrics (latency, throughput) to detect imbalance and dynamically steers incoming requests toward higher-performing containers within the same microservice. Rather than treating imbalance as a problem to eliminate through uniform scheduling, the system embraces it by exploiting performance heterogeneity: hot containers receive fewer requests and cool containers receive more, allowing the cluster to extract more useful work without additional provisioning. The approach integrates with existing cluster schedulers and load balancers.

title: Efficient Caching with A Tag-enhanced DRAM
problem: DRAM-based caches (e.g., HBM3-as-cache) suffer from high miss penalties due to two-step tag-then-data access, wasted data movement on cache misses where data is fetched then discarded, and interference between demand requests and miss-fetched data on the data bus. Existing DRAM cache designs cannot perform in-DRAM tag comparison or conditional data response, so they always transfer data regardless of hit/miss status.
method: TDRAM adds small, low-latency metadata/tag mats to an HBM3 die alongside the existing data mats, enabling lockstep tag-and-data access, in-DRAM tag comparison, and conditional data response (data is only transferred to the CPU if the comparison indicates a hit), eliminating wasted data bus transfers on misses. Opportunistic early tag probing allows tag lookups to start before the full row is available, reducing both hit and miss latencies. A flush buffer stores conflicting dirty data on write misses within the DRAM, eliminating data bus turnaround delays caused by writing back dirty evictees before fetching new data.

title: Reviving In-Storage Hardware Compression on ZNS SSDs through Host-SSD Collaboration
problem: Zoned Namespace (ZNS) SSDs cannot benefit from traditional host-transparent in-storage hardware compression because the ZNS interface's sequential write constraint makes it impossible to locate variable-length compressed chunks and reclaim the space freed by compression without exposing this information to the host.
method: CCZNS (Collaborative Compression for ZNS) decouples compression execution from indexing by introducing a new ZNS interface extension where the SSD hardware performs compression but exposes chunk boundaries and offset metadata to the host rather than hiding them. The host (e.g., RocksDB with ZenFS) uses this metadata to manage address mapping and space reclamation, while the SSD accelerates the compression compute. A case study on RocksDB/ZenFS demonstrates how the host software is adapted to consume CCZNS metadata.

title: Anda: Unlocking Efficient LLM Inference with a Variable-Length Grouped Activation Data Format
problem: Weight-only quantized LLMs retain floating-point (FP) activations for accuracy, which shifts the energy and latency bottleneck to costly FP memory accesses and FP-INT GEMM computation; existing LLM accelerators optimize computation alone without jointly addressing data representation and movement for FP activations.
method: Anda proposes a new adaptive activation data type with a group-shared exponent and dynamically allocated mantissa bits per group, enabling variable precision per LLM module. An iterative post-training precision search algorithm determines per-module bit-widths to balance accuracy and efficiency without retraining. On the hardware side, Anda uses a bit-plane-based data organization, bit-serial computation processing elements, and a runtime bit-plane compressor to simultaneously shrink storage, computation, and memory footprint. The result is a hardware-software co-designed accelerator targeting FP-INT GEMM in LLMs.

title: Virtuoso: Enabling Fast and Accurate Virtual Memory Research via an Imitation-based Operating System Simulation Methodology
problem: Existing virtual memory (VM) simulation tools either lack accuracy in modeling OS software components (e.g., page table walks, TLB shootdowns, OS scheduling interactions) or are too slow and complex to prototype hardware/OS co-designs spanning the hardware/software boundary.
method: Virtuoso introduces an imitation-based OS simulation methodology where a lightweight simulator imitates the behavior of a full OS by training on traces of OS decisions (page allocation, eviction, TLB management) captured from real OS runs, then replaying those decisions with hardware-accurate timing in a fast simulation framework. This enables rapid iteration over hardware/OS co-design points without full OS simulation overhead.
